name: BrowserRouter
desc: Provides the history object and the current location to the whole tree. Mount one per app, usually in main.jsx or at the top of App.
body:
Two other routers exist for two other problems.

`HashRouter` puts the path after `#` (`/app#/hotels`), so the server never sees it and no rewrite rule is needed. Use it only when the host cannot serve `index.html` for unknown paths.

`MemoryRouter` keeps the history in memory with no address bar at all, which is what tests want.

Never render a second `BrowserRouter` deeper in the tree. Each one creates its own history, so the inner router shows a different location than the outer one and links stop agreeing with the address bar.

name: Routes
desc: Picks the single best matching Route from its children and renders only that one.
example:
import { Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';

// Specificity decides, not the order in this JSX.
<Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/hotels" element={<Hotels />} />
    <Route path="/hotels/:hotel_id" element={<HotelDetail />} />
    <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
</Routes>
body:
React Router 5 used `Switch`, which took the first match in source order. `Routes` ranks instead: a static segment beats a dynamic one, and a dynamic one beats a splat. That is why `*` can sit first and still lose.

A `Routes` only renders one child. If two elements must appear at once, one of them belongs in the parent as layout, or the URL needs a nested route with `Outlet`.

name: Route
desc: Maps a path pattern to one element. Relative paths nest under the parent route and must not start with a slash.
example:
<Route path="/hotels" element={<HotelsLayout />}>
    {/* index: renders on /hotels exactly */}
    <Route index element={<HotelList />} />
    {/* relative: becomes /hotels/:hotel_id */}
    <Route path=":hotel_id" element={<HotelDetail />} />
    <Route path="*" element={<SectionNotFound />} />
</Route>
body:
`element` takes JSX, so props are free: `<Route path="/admin" element={<Admin role="owner" />} />`.

The 6.4 spelling `<Route path="/hotels" Component={Hotels} />` passes the component type instead and lets the data router keep the element mounted across param changes. Both work, `element` is the one to write in an exam.

The v4 and v5 `component={Hotels}` and `render={...}` props are gone. A lowercase `component` renders nothing and gives no warning.

name: index route
desc: The child that renders when the parent path matches exactly and no other child does.
example:
<Route path="/hotels" element={<HotelsLayout />}>
    {/* /hotels shows the list inside the layout outlet */}
    <Route index element={<HotelList />} />
    <Route path=":hotel_id" element={<HotelDetail />} />
</Route>
body:
`index` is a boolean flag, not a path. It cannot have children, because an index route is a leaf by definition.

Writing `<Route path="" element={...} />` in the same position does not match `/hotels` and is the usual cause of an empty page under a layout. Use `index`.

name: Link
desc: Renders an anchor and navigates on click without reloading the document.
body:
The rendered `<a>` carries a real `href`, so ctrl click, middle click and "open in new tab" behave normally. A plain `<a href>` reloads the page and drops React state, which is the bug `Link` prevents.

For a path built from parts, `to` also takes an object: `{ pathname: '/hotels', search: '?city=Eger' }`. String interpolation is shorter and reads fine for one param.

name: NavLink
desc: Link with an isActive flag for the current URL, used for menus and tab bars.
example:
// end stops '/hotels' from staying active on '/hotels/7'
<NavLink to="/" end className={({ isActive }) => (isActive ? 'nav on' : 'nav')}>
    Home
</NavLink>
<NavLink
    to="/hotels"
    style={({ isActive }) => ({ fontWeight: isActive ? 700 : 400 })}
>
    Hotels
</NavLink>
body:
The default match is a prefix match. `to="/hotels"` is active on `/hotels` and on `/hotels/7`. Add `end` when only the exact URL should count, and always add it on the home link, or `to="/"` matches every path.

`className` and `style` accept a function that receives `{ isActive, isPending }`, so no comparison against `useLocation().pathname` is needed.

name: Outlet
desc: Marks where the matched child route renders inside a parent route element.
body:
A parent route renders once and its children swap inside the outlet, so shared chrome does not remount on navigation.

Forgetting `<Outlet />` is the most common nested route bug: the URL changes, the parent renders, the child never appears, and the route table looks correct.

`useOutletContext` passes a value from parent to child without prop drilling, but props on the child element are usually simpler.

name: useParams()
desc: Returns the dynamic segments of the matched route as strings, or an empty object when the route has none.

name: useNavigate()
desc: Returns a function that navigates from code: after a POST, after a failed auth check, after a timeout.
body:
`{ replace: true }` keeps the page the user just left out of the history stack. Use it after login, after a delete, and after submitting a form, otherwise the back button returns to a page that no longer makes sense and a refresh repeats the action.

`state` lives in the history entry, not in the URL. It survives a refresh of that entry and is lost when the link is copied, so it suits "return where you came from" and nothing that must be shareable.

Read it with `useLocation().state` and guard the first visit: `location.state?.from?.pathname ?? '/'`.

name: useSearchParams()
desc: Reads and writes the query string as URLSearchParams, so a filter survives a refresh and can be shared as a link.
body:
`get` returns `null` when the key is absent and `''` for `?city=`. `getAll` returns repeated keys, which is what a set of checkboxes produces.

Values are encoded on write and decoded on read, so an accented city or a value with `&` needs no `encodeURIComponent`.

The setter also accepts a function of the previous params, and `{ replace: true }` keeps a search box that fires on every keystroke out of the history stack.

name: <Navigate>
desc: Redirects during render. The declarative form of a redirect, used by protected routes.

name: protected route
desc: A wrapper component that renders its children only when the user is signed in, otherwise redirects to login.
body:
Client side protection hides UI. It is not security: anyone can call `/api/admin` with curl. The API must verify the session on every request, and the route guard is only the part that avoids showing a broken page.

For a whole section, wrap the layout route instead of every child:

```jsx
<Route element={<RequireAuth><AdminLayout /></RequireAuth>}>
    <Route path="/admin" element={<Dashboard />} />
    <Route path="/admin/bookings" element={<Bookings />} />
</Route>
```

name: 404 route
desc: A splat route that catches every URL no other route matched.
example:
<Routes>
    <Route element={<Layout />}>
        <Route index element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="hotels" element={<Hotels />} />
        {/* root catch all, keeps the layout */}
        <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
    </Route>
</Routes>
body:
`*` matches one or more segments, including slashes, so it catches `/a/b/c`. Put it inside the layout route to keep the header on the error page.

A section can have its own 404 to keep its own chrome:

```jsx
<Route path="hotels" element={<HotelsLayout />}>
    <Route index element={<HotelList />} />
    <Route path=":hotel_id" element={<HotelDetail />} />
    <Route path="*" element={<SectionNotFound />} />
</Route>
```

Order in JSX does not matter, specificity does: `:hotel_id` beats `*`. If the section 404 never shows, a root `*` or a missing `Outlet` in the layout is the cause. Always put a `Link` home in the 404 body.

name: layout route
desc: A route with no path that carries shared chrome and renders its children in an outlet.
example:
<Routes>
    {/* no path: matches whatever the children match */}
    <Route element={<Layout />}>
        <Route index element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="hotels" element={<Hotels />} />
        <Route path="search" element={<HotelSearch />} />
        <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
    </Route>
</Routes>
body:
Pathless routes are how a header, sidebar or footer is written once. Children use relative paths, so `hotels` becomes `/hotels` at the root level.

Layouts nest: a pathless `Layout` can hold a `/hotels` route that has its own `HotelsLayout`, each with an `Outlet`. The order of the outlets decides where the page lands.

A layout route is not the same as an `index` route. An index route is a leaf that fills the parent outlet, a layout route is a parent that provides one.

name: search param encoding
desc: URLSearchParams percent encodes on write and decodes on read, so accents, spaces and ampersands survive the round trip.
body:
Do not call `encodeURIComponent` before `setSearchParams` or before `new URLSearchParams`. The value is encoded twice, the server reads `%2526`, and the bug looks like a server problem.

A space is written as `+` in a query string and read back as a space, together with `%20`. That is form encoding and it is correct.

When building a fetch URL, use the same class:

```jsx
const query = new URLSearchParams({ city, stars });
fetch(`/api/hotels?${query}`);
```

Repeated keys come from `append`, not `set`, and are read with `getAll`.
